name: Omar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run about six hundred ewes on hill land, most of it rough grazing up on the fell, which is the open high ground above the farm. In winter I'm out on the quad bike at first light with the two dogs, Bess and Fly, checking the ewes, putting out feed blocks and looking for any stuck in a ditch. I love the hill in the morning, when the cloud's below you. What wears me down is the price at the autumn lamb sales, and my knees, which are fifty-eight and feel eighty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is in the picture at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Maria cooks school dinners at the primary school in the village, she's been there twenty years. Our son Daniel is in the army, and our daughter Sara works at a bank in the city. Neither of them will take the sheep on, and I've made my peace with that, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, let it be a tool and nothing more. I use one now and then myself, I asked it once what was causing lameness in my hoggs, the young sheep, and it gave me a decent list. But it doesn't walk the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing. Sheep still need gathering, the weather still decides everything, and the lamb price is still set by the big buyers. It's a handy encyclopaedia, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. Maybe I'd use it to help with the subsidy forms, which I hate, if Sara set it up for me. The big job this year would be rebuilding a stretch of dry stone wall that came down in the storm, which takes me about three weeks with a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like any other year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it gave you a decent list about the lameness. Did you act on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I took the list to the vet, Mrs Kowalski, and she crossed off half of it and laughed at one. But the other half was right, and it saved me a call-out. That's about what I'd expect: useful if someone who knows checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps you with the wall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Jim from the next farm, he's seventy-three and better at walling than me. We do it together every few years and he tells the same stories every time. It wouldn't be the same with anybody else.

S0.say: Let it be a tool and nothing more, because it doesn't walk the hill. I use one now and then, and it gave me a decent list once about lameness in my young sheep.
S0.think: For me it changes almost nothing, because sheep still need gathering, weather decides everything and big buyers set the lamb price. It's a handy encyclopaedia, that's all.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and perhaps uses the assistant for subsidy forms if Sara sets it up. Spends about three weeks rebuilding a storm-damaged dry stone wall with his neighbour Jim.
S0.quote: That's about what I'd expect: useful if someone who knows checks it.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is a steady, occasional user who treats AI as an encyclopaedia that needs a vet to check it. His world is the fell, the weather and the lamb sales, and his neighbour Jim. He has accepted, mostly, that his children won't take the sheep on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the companies to decide who they hire, but young people need a start, and apprenticeships are the way. I've always said that, and the young farmers' club agrees. Less talk about degrees and more about learning a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow means I'm nearly done before it really matters. I'm thinking about the next ten years, maybe cutting the flock as my knees go. The hiring bit worries me for the young lads round here who would have gone into the town's offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take on a young lad from the village to help at lambing and gathering, paid, and teach him what Jim taught me. Maybe three or four thousand a year. And I'd keep using the assistant now and then for the bits I find hard, like the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the young ones. For me, steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cutting the flock as your knees go. How many ewes is the right number for you at sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three hundred. That's what I can gather with the dogs and one helper without killing myself. The hill would still be grazed, just more lightly, which the conservation people would like anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hill farming relies a lot on subsidy money. How does that sit with you, given what you've said about handouts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits awkwardly, I'll admit. But I'd say it's payment for looking after the land, the walls, the hill, not a handout. Without it there'd be no sheep up there, and then the bracken takes over in five years.

S1.say: It's for companies to decide who they hire, but young people need a start, and apprenticeships are the way. Less talk about degrees and more about learning a trade.
S1.think: Slow means I'm nearly done before it really matters, and I'm already thinking about cutting the flock as my knees go. The hiring part worries me for local lads who would have gone into the town's offices.
S1.do: Takes on a local lad for lambing and gathering at about three or four thousand a year and teaches him what Jim taught him. Keeps using the assistant now and then for paperwork.
S1.feel: Uneasy for young people, steady for himself.
S1.quote: Without it there'd be no sheep up there, and then the bracken takes over in five years.
S1.fieldNote: When asked gently about relying on subsidies while opposing handouts, he admits the awkwardness and reframes it as payment for looking after land. He plans to scale down to three hundred ewes as his knees go. He wants young people taught a trade, the way he was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the politicians shouting doesn't help anyone, and the government shouldn't just hand out money. But companies that make a fortune by cutting jobs have a duty to the towns they took from. I'd say that at the mart, which is what we call the livestock market, over a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Sara I think about. Bank office work is what you'd call routine, and she's not senior. The farm doesn't change, but if Sara loses her job in the city, with the rent she pays, she'd struggle quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sara she can come home any time, and we'd help with rent for a few months if needed, maybe from the two or three months of savings we've got. I'd put off buying a new quad bike, the old one can manage. And I'd keep the lad on, because he's not going to find office work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Sara. The sheep don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd help Sara with rent from your savings. How many months could you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three, maybe four if Maria and I tightened up. Our savings are there for a bad winter on the hill, when we have to buy in hay. If we used them for Sara and then had a hard winter, we'd be borrowing, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Sara on the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, come home for a bit, love, your mother would like it. I wouldn't say I'm worried, I'd let her mother say that. And I'd tell her the hill doesn't care what job you've got.

S2.say: Politicians shouting doesn't help, and the government shouldn't just hand out money. But companies making a fortune from cutting jobs have a duty to the towns they took from.
S2.think: It's Sara I think about, because bank office work is routine and she's not senior. The farm doesn't change, but with her city rent she'd struggle quickly.
S2.do: Tells Sara she can come home and offers three or four months of rent help from savings meant for buying hay in a hard winter. Puts off a new quad bike and keeps the young helper on.
S2.feel: Anxious for Sara, while the sheep carry on regardless.
S2.quote: I wouldn't say I'm worried, I'd let her mother say that.
S2.fieldNote: His savings have a clear purpose, a bad winter's hay, so helping his daughter means a real trade-off he names honestly. He keeps the young helper on as a quiet act of loyalty. His traditional view puts duty on companies to the towns rather than on government handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people making fortunes from this should put something back into the communities, not through handouts but jobs and training. The political crisis wouldn't surprise me, people are angry when they see others getting rich while they lose their jobs. Hill farms would still be here, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it might even be a bit better for us. People losing city jobs might buy cheaper lamb, and some might want to come and live in the countryside. But house prices booming means the cottages in the valley become holiday homes, and the young lads can't afford to live here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the sheep, and I'd offer the cottage at the bottom of the farm to the lad who helps me, at a low rent, before some city buyer offers silly money for it. I'd tell Sara again she can come home. And I'd say a prayer for the country, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My work would be fine, but the valley would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd turn down silly money for the cottage. How silly would it have to be before you'd think again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it paid for our retirement outright, I'd think about it, I'm not a saint. But the lad needs somewhere to live, or he leaves, and then who helps me gather? Money in the bank doesn't fetch sheep off the fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in the valley you'd worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young families. When I was a boy there were eleven children on the school bus from this valley, now there's three. If the cottages go to holiday lets, Maria's school will lose more.

S3.say: The people making fortunes should put something back into communities through jobs and training, not handouts. People get angry when others get rich while they lose jobs, but hill farms would still be here.
S3.think: It might even be a bit better for us, with people buying cheaper lamb and some moving to the countryside. But booming house prices turn the valley cottages into holiday homes, and the young lads can't afford to live here.
S3.do: Offers the farm's bottom cottage to his young helper at a low rent before a city buyer can bid for it. Repeats his offer for Sara to come home.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because his work would be fine but the valley would change.
S3.quote: Money in the bank doesn't fetch sheep off the fell.
S3.fieldNote: He sees the fast scenario through housing in his valley rather than through his own job. He admits a sale price could tempt him, which makes his choice to house his helper more credible. Falling numbers on the school bus are his measure of the community's health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on flat farms maybe, but they'll struggle on the hill, and I'd say that with some pride. But I'd also say the country can't just throw people out of work in a few years without something breaking. Help should come through jobs and families, not a cheque in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm less sure than I'd sound. They already sell collars that keep sheep in an area without fences, and drones that can count a flock. Put those with a robot that can climb, and a big landowner wouldn't need a shepherd. And Maria's school kitchen, that's exactly where robots would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd watch what the bigger farms did, and if the collars worked on a neighbour's flock for a season, I'd maybe try them on part of mine. I'd talk to Maria about what we'd live on if her job went. And I'd think hard about cutting to three hundred ewes earlier than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. For Maria more than me. And I'm proud and scared at the same time, which is a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say it with pride but you're less sure privately. Which is true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. A robot might manage a flat field. Send it up Black Crag in February sleet and I'll go and fetch it down, same as I fetch the ewes. But I said the same about quad bikes once, and now I can't live without mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if Maria's job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose about a third of what we live on. She'd be lost without the children, she loves those kids. I'd probably have her up on the hill with me, she's better with a lamb than she lets on.

S4.say: Robots might work on flat farms, but they'll struggle on the hill. The country can't throw people out of work in a few years without something breaking, and help should come through jobs and families, not a cheque in the post.
S4.think: I'm less sure than I sound, because collars that keep sheep in without fences and drones that count flocks already exist, and with a climbing robot a big landowner wouldn't need a shepherd. Maria's school kitchen is exactly where robots would go.
S4.do: Watches bigger farms and tries the collars on part of his flock only after they've worked on a neighbour's for a season. Talks with Maria about losing a third of their income if her job goes and considers cutting to three hundred ewes earlier than planned.
S4.feel: Alarmed, more for Maria than himself, and both proud and scared at once.
S4.quote: A robot might manage a flat field. Send it up Black Crag in February sleet and I'll go and fetch it down, same as I fetch the ewes.
S4.fieldNote: There is a clear gap between his public pride about the hill and his private knowledge of shepherding tech that already exists. He resolves it by admitting both are true and recalling his own change of heart over quad bikes. His wife's school kitchen job is his biggest worry here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because of Maria's job and because I'm not as sure about the hill as I let on. What would help is keeping the land payments for hill farmers, and apprenticeships so young people can learn the work. And time, a few years for people like Maria to find something else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. Bess and Fly do more work than any machine I've owned, and they don't need charging. A robot might manage a flat field. Send it up Black Crag in February sleet and I'll go and fetch it down, same as I fetch the ewes.

headlineQuote: A robot might manage a flat field. Send it up Black Crag in February sleet and I'll go and fetch it down, same as I fetch the ewes.
portrait: Omar Santos is a 58-year-old hill sheep farmer with about six hundred ewes, two dogs and knees that are starting to give out, married to Maria, who cooks school dinners. He uses AI now and then as an encyclopaedia but trusts his vet to check it, and he copies new tools only after a neighbour has proved them. He opposes handouts but admits that subsidy payments for hill land sit awkwardly with that. Across the scenarios he worries for his daughter's bank job and the valley's young families, and in the robot scenario he is proud of the hill in public but privately unsure, and most afraid for Maria's job.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because Maria's school kitchen job is exposed and he is less sure than he sounds that the hill would stay safe.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping land payments for hill farmers, apprenticeships for young people, and a few years' time for people like Maria to find other work.
